title: Operations and pointed refinements of normalized finite splittings
statement:
Let $u:X\to U$ be a pro-etale covering of schemes with $X$ nonempty and connected, fix a geometric point $z$ of $X$, and let a profinite abelian group $G$ act over $U$ with comparison $X[G]\cong X\times_UX$, $(x,g)\mapsto(x,gx)$ [def-weil-pbc-proetale-site], [def-weil-geometric-point], [def-sfb-profinite-test-objects]. Let $\mathcal L$ be the full subcategory of set sheaves on $U_{\mathrm{proet}}$ whose pullbacks to $X$ are constant finite sheaves. Suppose their fibre-normalized splittings $\phi_F:F|_X\cong\underline{F_{u(z)}}_X$ are unique and natural in sheaf maps, and their descent arrows are $(x,g,v)\mapsto(x,g,g\cdot v)$ for continuous actions on the finite fibres [def-weil-proetale-geometric-stalk], [def-weil-pbc-constant-sheaf].

The category $\mathcal L$ is closed under finite products and contains the terminal sheaf. The normalized splittings preserve those products and the terminal object. If $R$ is a finite ring and $M$ is a sheaf of left $R$-modules whose underlying set sheaf is in $\mathcal L$, its finite fibre is an $R$-module and the $G$-action is $R$-linear; normalized splittings identify zero, addition, negation and every scalar multiplication on all local sections [def-weil-sheaf-of-modules-category]. For any homomorphism of finite rings $a:R\to R'$, restriction of scalars preserves these identifications. The sheaf $N$ obtained by sheafifying $R'\otimes_R M$ belongs to $\mathcal L$ and has canonical comparison
$$R'\otimes_R M_{u(z)}\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }N_{u(z)},$$
normalized by $b\otimes\operatorname{germ}(m)\mapsto\operatorname{germ}(b\otimes m)$. Its constant comparison over $X$ is given by the same formula and is $G$-equivariant for $g(b\otimes q)=b\otimes gq$; it is natural in module maps and compatible with composition of coefficient homomorphisms.

Let also $u':X'\to U'$ be such a connected pointed cover with group $G'$, point $z'$, and normalized splittings. Suppose maps $h:U'\to U$, $v:X'\to X$ and $\theta:G'\to G$ satisfy $uv=hu'$, $v(z')=z$ and $v(g'x')=\theta(g')v(x')$, and their induced maps commute with both projections of the torsor comparisons. For every $F\in\mathcal L$, $h^*F$ is trivialized by $X'$; under the pointed fibre identification its normalized splitting is the pullback of $\phi_F$, its action is restricted along $\theta$, and its full descent arrow is the pullback of that for $F$. These identifications commute with compositions of such pointed refinements [def-weil-proetale-inverse-image]. Pullbacks and sheafification use [def-weil-pbc-sheafification]. For arbitrary (possibly noncommutative) coefficient rings, left scalar extension has the balanced left-adjoint meaning of [def-pod-ring-scalar-extension].

source.place: Bhatt-Scholze Section 5.1, pp.34-35; agent-formulated finite operations, stalk tensor comparison, and pointed pullback uniqueness consequence of normalized descent.

proof.text: For a finite discrete diagram F of sheaves trivialized by W, choose finite sets A_j and their given isomorphisms after inverse image. The functor C from finite sets to sheaves on W, given by inclusion into sets, universe lift and constant sheaf, preserves finite limits: the first two functors preserve limits and set sheafification is left exact. Inverse image along W also preserves finite limits by det-pe-topos-functoriality-inverse-image. The natural isomorphism from C(A_j) to the inverse-image diagram identifies the inverse image of lim F with C(lim A_j), so lim F remains finite constant. This includes the empty diagram. Closure under isomorphism and finite products gives finite products in the full subcategory and preservation by its inclusion. The restricted stalk preserves these products because evaluation and sheaf inclusion preserve limits and its filtered neighbourhood colimit commutes with finite limits.

source.place: Section 5.1, pp.34-35, finite constant sheaves; general finite-limit calculation using Stacks 00WJ and filtered stalks.

proof.text: The forgetful functor from continuous finite G-actions to universe-lifted sets reflects limits: the continuous-action subcategory inclusion is fully faithful, the action forgetful functor reflects limits, and the finite-set inclusion and universe lift are fully faithful. The supplied natural fibreIso identifies the composite of fibre with this forgetful functor with the restricted stalk. The stalk preserves finite products by Step 1, hence reflection forces fibre itself to preserve finite products, including the terminal object. Thus this categorical assertion needs neither a new uniqueness argument for the normalized sections nor new descent lemmas; the supplied naturality still supplies the equations with product projections.

source.place: Section 5.1, pp.34-35; uniqueness hypothesis, product projections.

proof.text: Apply the stalk construction to the module laws of $M$: addition and scalar multiplication are computed on representatives after a common pointed refinement, so $Q=M_y$ is a left $R$-module. Each map $0:1\to M$, $+:M\times M\to M$, $-:M\to M$ and $r:M\to M$ is a map in $\mathcal L$. Naturality of $\phi$ for these maps, together with Step 2, identifies each operation on every local section with the same operation on constant labels. The descent comparison commutes with these sheaf maps, so its label map satisfies $g0=0$, $g(q+q')=gq+gq'$ and $g(rq)=r(gq)$. Thus the stipulated continuous finite action is $R$-linear.

source.place: Section 5.1, pp.34-35; finite module consequence of normalized descent.

proof.text: Restriction of scalars leaves the underlying set sheaf definitionally unchanged. Thus the original finite-constancy witness hM also witnesses finite constancy of the restricted sheaf, and its normalized universal section is heterogeneously equal by reflexivity to the original one. Apply normalizedFiniteSplittings_module for the S-module M, keep its label equivalence and label equation, and specialize its scalar-operation equation to a(r). This proves the restriction assertion without any new theorem or new hypothesis.

source.place: Finite coefficient consequence; balanced left coefficients, Stacks sites-modules.tex Tag 03CZ.

proof.text:
Apply the geometric scalar comparison to $u$, using its geometric inverse image and its canonical constant left-module lift. With $Q=M_y$, the linear splitting from Step 3 and the constant-module comparison give
$$N|_X\cong R'\otimes_R(M|_X)\cong R'\otimes_R\underline Q_X\cong\underline{R'\otimes_RQ}_X.$$
Every displayed comparison sends the local pure tensor to the pure tensor with the same coefficient and the same finite label. This is a finite constant sheaf: the map $(R')^Q\to R'\otimes_RQ$, $(b_q)\mapsto\sum_q b_q\otimes q$, is surjective, since all sums of pure tensors can be grouped by $q\in Q$. Both $R'$ and $Q$ are finite. Thus $N\in\mathcal L$; no flatness, freeness or commutativity is used.

source.place: Section 5.1, pp.34-35; scalar sheafification calculation, using the general left-scalar geometric comparison.

proof.text:
Let $P(V)=R'\otimes_RM(V)$ before sheafification. The pointed index of the stalk is small in the larger universe and filtered. Left scalar extension is a left adjoint to restriction by its defining universal property, so preservation of colimits gives
$$R'\otimes_R M_y\cong\varinjlim_{(V,\bar v)}(R'\otimes_RM(V)).$$
The sheafification-stalk theorem identifies the right side with $N_y$, using the underlying abelian presheaf of $P$. Operations pass through the colimit, so the resulting isomorphism $\beta$ is $R'$-linear. Since both comparisons are induced by their coprojections, $\beta(b\otimes\operatorname{germ}m)=\operatorname{germ}(b\otimes m)$. This also proves naturality in module maps. For the naturality assertion in Lean no choice of the comparison is needed: take any two comparison structures satisfying the germ equations. Scalar extension is a left adjoint, so the images of all stalk coprojections form a colimit cocone. Precompose the proposed naturality square with each such coprojection. The naturality equation for the induced colimit map and the two supplied germ equations reduce the square to naturality of the sheafification unit at that neighbourhood. Colimit extensionality now proves the square. In particular the proof uses no new scalar-extension or sheafification-stalk existence assumption.

source.place: Section 5.1, pp.34-35; agent stalk calculation using Stacks scalar adjunction and stalk-preserving sheafification.

proof.text: Let $\alpha:\underline{R'\otimes_RQ}_X\to N|_X$ be the inverse of the composite in Step 5. Under the canonical identification $(u^{-1}N)_z\cong N_y$, its stalk is $\beta$ of Step 6: both send $b\otimes\operatorname{germ}m$ to the germ of the sheafification-unit tensor. Thus $\alpha\circ\underline\beta^{-1}:\underline{N_y}_X\to N|_X$ is normalized to the identity at $z$. Uniqueness in the hypothesis makes it $\phi_N^{-1}$. Consequently the constant comparison of Step 5 is exactly the normalized one, with the asserted formula on all local sections.

source.place: Section 5.1, pp.34-35; fibre normalization, not a choice of an arbitrary tensor isomorphism.

proof.text:
On the overlap $X[G]$, apply scalar extension to the two pullbacks of $M$ and its descent arrow, using the natural geometric scalar comparisons of Step 5 for the two projections. Its value on a local pure tensor is
$$(x,g,b\otimes q)\longmapsto(x,g,b\otimes gq).$$
Pure tensors locally generate the sheafification, so this is equality of sheaf arrows on the entire overlap. Step 7 identifies these labels with the normalized fibre labels, proving $G$-equivariance. For $R\xrightarrow aR'\xrightarrow dR''$, both successive comparisons send $c\otimes(b\otimes m)$ to the germ or constant label of $c\,d(b)\otimes m$. Those generators generate the successive scalar extension, so the comparisons commute with coefficient composition. For a module map $t$ the two composites both send $b\otimes m$ to $b\otimes t(m)$, proving the remaining naturality.

source.place: Section 5.1, pp.34-35; explicit scalar descent and coefficient associativity on generators.

proof.text: The equality $uv=hu'$ and the inverse-image compositors identify $u'^{-1}h^{-1}F$ with $v^{-1}u^{-1}F$. Pulling $\phi_F$ back along $v$ therefore gives a splitting by the constant sheaf with value $Q_F$. Here inverse image preserves constant set sheaves: they are sheaf coproducts of copies of the terminal sheaf, and inverse image preserves both that object and all colimits. The natural stalk comparison identifies $(h^{-1}F)_{u'(z')}$ with $F_{u(z)}$; because $v(z')=z$, the pulled-back splitting has identity on this fibre. Thus $h^{-1}F$ lies in the analogous category on $U'$, and uniqueness there identifies its splitting with the pulled-back $\phi_F$.

source.place: Section 5.1, pp.34-35; pointed refinement by uniqueness and inverse-image composition.

proof.text:
By the two stipulated projection identities, the map of overlaps is, in the given torsor coordinates, $(x',g')\mapsto(v(x'),\theta(g'))$. Pull the whole descent arrow back along this map and use the splitting identified in Step 9. Substitution in its assumed formula gives
$$(x',g',q)\longmapsto(x',g',\theta(g')\cdot q).$$
This is substitution in morphisms of sheaves, and is valid on every test object and every local section, not merely on geometric stalks. Its label action is restriction along $\theta$, as claimed.

source.place: Section 5.1, pp.34-35; pointed equivariance and both projections of the supplied torsor comparison.

proof.text: For two pointed refinements, either pullback construction is a normalized splitting at the composite chosen point, so uniqueness identifies it with the splitting of the composite. The canonical inverse-image compositors make the domains identical; all maps are the adjunction-compatible ones. In the overlap formulas the two substitutions replace $g''$ by $\theta(\theta'(g''))$, which is exactly the substitution for the composite. Hence both splittings and full descent arrows commute with composition. Identity refinements give identity maps by the same normalization.

source.place: Section 5.1, pp.34-35; uniqueness and the explicit composite overlap formula.
